Galactic bulge

Words: 35
Galaxy OurBigBook.com
A galactic bulge is a centrally concentrated stellar population in a galaxy, usually thicker than its disk. Its origin, rotation and random stellar motions can differ from those of the disk; bulge light is often described by a Sérsic profile.

Stellar halo

Words: 126 Articles: 2
Galaxy OurBigBook.com
A stellar halo is the extended, approximately spheroidal stellar population surrounding a galaxy. It differs from the total dark matter halo. If its outer luminosity density is r−p, its projected light follows the projection of a spherical power-law emissivity and scales as R1−p away from breaks and outer truncation.

Intracluster light

Words: 42
Stellar halo OurBigBook.com
Intracluster light comes from stars bound to a cluster rather than an individual galaxy. Tidal stripping and disruption of member systems can create extended diffuse light and substructure. Distinguishing this component from the outer envelope of the central galaxy depends on the adopted dynamical or photometric definition.

Stellar stream

Words: 46
Stellar halo OurBigBook.com
A stellar stream is a correlated collection of stars commonly originating in the disruption of a bound progenitor. Phase mixing can erase spatial contrast while leaving coherence in orbital integrals. Such fossil debris constrains a galaxy's past accretion, although not every stream is from a galaxy: star clusters also produce streams.

Star-forming galaxy

Words: 26
Galaxy OurBigBook.com
A star-forming galaxy is a galaxy with ongoing star formation. Its hot young stars can supply hydrogen-ionizing radiation to the intergalactic medium, with the contribution controlled by the ionizing photon escape fraction.

Irregular galaxy

Words: 24
Galaxy OurBigBook.com
An irregular galaxy lacks a regular spiral or elliptical outline. Many contain substantial gas and recent star formation; irregular appearance alone does not determine a stellar population's age.

Spiral galaxy

Words: 18
Galaxy OurBigBook.com
A spiral galaxy has a galactic disk with spiral structure, commonly cold interstellar gas and ongoing star formation as well as an older stellar population.

Galactic disk

Words: 420 Articles: 7
Galaxy OurBigBook.com
A galactic disk is a flattened stellar or gaseous component of a galaxy, commonly supported mainly by ordered rotation. Its radial mass profile determines its galaxy rotation curve; thickness, truncation and external forces also matter. A galactic disk need not be an exponential galactic disk, and its neutral-gas absorption radius need not equal a stellar scale length.

Thin galactic disk

Words: 40
Galactic disk OurBigBook.com
A thin galactic disk is a stellar component whose vertical extent is small compared with its radial size. Small vertical velocity dispersion and substantial specific angular momentum are characteristic. Its survival constrains cumulative galactic disk heating, but its stars need not all have the same formation epoch.

Galactic disk heating

Words: 32
Galactic disk OurBigBook.com
Galactic disk heating increases the random velocities of stars through encounters with molecular clouds, nonaxisymmetric gravitational disturbances, and other perturbations. Older stellar populations usually have larger velocity dispersions and greater vertical thickness, although birth conditions and migration also affect the relation.

Galactic disk flaring

Words: 47
Galactic disk OurBigBook.com
Galactic disk flaring is an outward increase of vertical thickness. A constant vertical velocity dispersion in an approximately thin-sheet stellar Newtonian gravitational field gives h∝1/Σ∗​. An exponential galactic disk then predicts h∝eR/Rd​ for a gas tracer. Inside a thick stellar layer the potential is instead approximately harmonic, and the tracer width is σz​/νz​ with vertical epicyclic frequency νz​.

Self-gravitating isothermal slab (ρ(z)=ρ0​sech2(z/z0​))

Words: 252 Articles: 3
Galactic disk OurBigBook.com
A plane-symmetric, self-gravitating stellar population with constant vertical velocity dispersion satisfies the vertical Jeans equation and the Poisson equation for Newtonian gravity. With Φ′(0)=0, their solution is
ρ=ρ0​sech2(z/z0​),Φ−Φ(0)=2σz2​logcosh(z/z0​),z02​=2πGρ0​σz2​​.
(1)
Its surface density is Σ=2ρ0​z0​, so z0​=σz2​/(πGΣ). Its outer density tail is exponential with scale height z0​/2; its central profile is not exponential.

Orbits in a self-gravitating isothermal slab (Φ(z)−Φ(0)=2σ2logcosh(z/H))

Words: 78
Self-gravitating isothermal slab OurBigBook.com
For a self-gravitating isothermal slab with ρ=ρ0​sech2(z/H) and H2=σ2/(2πGρ0​), hydrostatic equilibrium gives the displayed Newtonian gravitational potential. A test particle has constant in-plane velocity and conserved vertical energy Ez​=z˙2/2+Φ(z)−Φ(0). Its vertical motion is periodic for every finite Ez​>0, with turning height Harcoshexp[Ez​/(2σ2)]. Near the plane it is a harmonic oscillator of squared frequency 4πGρ0​; at large height the force tends to the constant 2πGΣ, where Σ=2ρ0​H. The ideal infinite slab has no finite vertical escape energy.

Isothermal displacement energy of a self-gravitating slab (ω2I=cs2​∫∣δρ∣2/ρdz−(4πG)−1∫(∣ϕz​∣2+k2∣ϕ∣2)dz)

Words: 130 Articles: 1
Self-gravitating isothermal slab OurBigBook.com
For an isothermal gas slab, a horizontal Fourier mode has δρ=−ikρξx​−(ρξz​)z​, W=cs2​δρ/ρ+ϕ, ω2ξx​=ikW, ω2ξz​=Wz​ and (∂z2​−k2)ϕ=4πGδρ. Multiply momentum by ρξ∗ and integrate by parts, then use the Poisson equation for Newtonian gravity. Vanishing pressure-work and gravitational boundary terms give the displayed real quadratic identity, with I=∫ρ∣ξ∣2dz>0. Thus every admissible squared eigenfrequency is real; a negative value gives gravitational growth rather than an oscillatory instability.
Marginal fragmentation mode of an isothermal slab (∣k∣H=1,ϕ∝sech(z/H))
Words: 67
Isothermal displacement energy of a self-gravitating slab OurBigBook.com
For mass density ρ=ρ0​sech2(z/H) with H2=cs2​/(2πGρ0​), a zero-frequency gravitational mode with k=0 obeys W=0. Its potential satisfies ϕzz​+[2sech2(z/H)/H2−k2]ϕ=0. The substitution τ=tanh(z/H) gives the associated Legendre differential equation of degree one and order ∣k∣H. Solutions decaying at both infinities exist only at ∣k∣H=1, when ϕ∝sech(z/H). Longer horizontal wavelengths are unstable. Neutral mass-preserving relabeling displacements and the uniform vertical translation at k=0 are distinct from this fragmentation threshold.

Galaxy stellar mass (M∗​)

Words: 430 Articles: 8
Galaxy OurBigBook.com
Galaxy stellar mass is the total mass in a galaxy's stars and stellar remnants. It is usually inferred from luminosity and colour or a spectral-energy-distribution fit, so it depends on stellar-population models, dust treatment, and the adopted initial mass function.

Mass-to-light ratio (Υ=M/L)

Words: 187 Articles: 2
Galaxy stellar mass OurBigBook.com
The mass-to-light ratio compares the mass assigned to an astronomical system with its luminosity in a specified band, often in solar units. A stellar value uses only stellar mass and depends on the stellar population, age, composition and band. A dynamical value can include gas and dark matter, so it need not equal the stellar value. In a halo-to-galaxy mapping, L=M∗​/Υ∗​ requires the stellar ratio and not the total dark matter halo ratio.

Aperture dependence of mass-to-light ratio (Υ(<R)=M(<R)/L(<R))

Words: 70
Mass-to-light ratio OurBigBook.com
A dynamical mass-to-light ratio must specify its aperture and whether the mass includes dark matter. A growing dark halo can increase Υ(<R) outside the bright stellar body even when the stellar ratio is constant. Comparing a tidal-radius satellite mass with a large-aperture host mass is different from comparing both within their half-light radii. From M∝σ2R and L∝σ4, the inferred ratio scales as R/σ2, so equal ratios additionally require homologous radius scaling.

Mass-to-light ratio of a power-law stellar population

Words: 50
Mass-to-light ratio OurBigBook.com
Write x=m/M⊙​, the initial mass function as dN=Ax−αdx, and a main-sequence mass-luminosity relation as L/L⊙​=xβ. On a<x<b, the mass-to-light ratio in solar units is
M⊙​/L⊙​Υ​=∫ab​xβ−αdx∫ab​x1−αdx​.
(2)
For α=β=3 this is exactly 1/(ab). The result concerns the specified unevolved stellar population; stellar remnants, evolved luminous stars and cooling substellar objects require different accounting.

Galaxy stellar mass function (dngal​/dM∗​)

Words: 178 Articles: 3
Galaxy stellar mass OurBigBook.com
The galaxy stellar mass function counts galaxies per stellar-mass interval and volume, often using comoving volume. Its stellar-mass moment gives the cosmic stellar mass density, while its number moment counts galaxies only if the low-mass population is integrable or truncated. It differs from the initial mass function of individual stars.

Cosmic stellar mass density (ρ∗com​=∫0∞​M∗​n∗​(M∗​)dM∗​)

Words: 46
Galaxy stellar mass function OurBigBook.com
The cosmic stellar mass density is the mass moment of a galaxy stellar mass function in a stated volume convention. With a comoving mass function it is mass per comoving volume, while proper density is larger by (1+z)3. Comparing it to a critical or matter density requires keeping the epoch and volume convention explicit.

Stellar mass function with a square-root exponential cutoff (n∗​(M∗​)∝M∗−7/4​e−M∗​/M∗,ch​​)

Words: 90 Articles: 1
Galaxy stellar mass function OurBigBook.com
A generalized mass function with low-mass slope −7/4 and cutoff e−M∗​/M∗,ch​​ differs from the ordinary exponential Schechter cutoff. Its total stellar-mass density is finite, even though its untruncated total galaxy count diverges. This form arises from a scale-free Press-Schechter mass function with a constant stellar-to-halo mass mapping.
Stellar mass density from a square-root exponential cutoff (ρ∗​=2π​ϕch​M∗,ch​)
Words: 42
Stellar mass function with a square-root exponential cutoff OurBigBook.com
Integrating galactic stellar mass against a x−7/4e−x​ mass function requires ∫0∞​x−3/4e−x​dx. Substitution u=x​ turns it into 2Γ(1/2)=2π​. Thus the stellar density is 2π​ times characteristic number density times characteristic galactic stellar mass, in the same volume convention as the mass function.

Gas-to-stellar mass ratio (rg​=Mg​/M∗​)

Words: 30
Galaxy OurBigBook.com
The gas-to-stellar mass ratio compares a galaxy's gas reservoir with its stellar mass. Different observational definitions may include only molecular gas, only atomic gas, or both with a helium correction.

Galaxy evolution

Words: 2k Articles: 49
Galaxy OurBigBook.com
Galaxy evolution studies how galaxies acquire mass, form stars, enrich their gas, exchange material with their surroundings, change morphology, and merge over cosmic time.

Galaxy morphological evolution

Words: 37
Galaxy evolution OurBigBook.com
Galaxy morphological evolution changes the relative prevalence and internal structure of discs, spheroids, bars, and irregular systems over time. Comparing epochs requires consistent wavelength, spatial resolution, and selection. Galaxy mergers, gas accretion and internal instabilities can all contribute.

Galaxy size evolution

Words: 50
Galaxy evolution OurBigBook.com
The observed size distribution of galaxies changes with epoch at a given galaxy stellar mass. Growth of an individual object and changes in which objects enter a selected sample both contribute. Minor galaxy mergers can deposit stars at large radii, increasing size while adding relatively little mass; stellar mass loss and dissipative evolution provide other mechanisms.

Galaxy red sequence

Words: 48
Galaxy evolution OurBigBook.com
A galaxy red sequence is the relatively narrow red locus in a galaxy colour-magnitude diagram, populated largely by systems with little recent star formation. Its colour, abundance, and galaxy stellar mass evolve. Dust and selection must be distinguished from old stellar ages; growth can involve quenching and later assembly of existing stars.

Starburst galaxy

Words: 39
Galaxy evolution OurBigBook.com
A starburst galaxy undergoes an episode of rapid star formation. An instantaneous-burst idealization places all newly formed stars at one stellar age, so their present evolutionary-state fractions follow from the initial mass function at that fixed age rather than from an average over formation times.

Galaxy merger

Words: 434 Articles: 9
Galaxy evolution OurBigBook.com
A galaxy merger combines two or more galaxies into a remnant. Their orbital angular momentum and energy are redistributed into internal stellar and halo motions, escaping matter, and, when present, dissipative gas. A bound pair produced by tidal capture of galaxies need not coalesce immediately.

Gas-rich galaxy merger

Words: 40
Galaxy merger OurBigBook.com
A gas-rich galaxy merger involves a substantial reservoir of gas capable of radiative cooling. Dissipation and gravitational torques permit gas inflow and enhanced star formation, unlike the nearly collisionless stellar evolution in a dry galaxy merger. A surviving or replenished gas reservoir can subsequently form a galactic disk.

Major galaxy merger

Words: 42
Galaxy merger OurBigBook.com
A major galaxy merger joins galaxies with comparable masses. Rapid changes in the gravitational potential can redistribute stellar orbital energies through violent relaxation, substantially disturbing preexisting galactic disks. The outcome depends on gas content, orbit and subsequent accretion; a major merger does not universally prohibit disk rebuilding.

Galaxy merger OurBigBook.com
A target galaxy with geometric encounter cross section πR2 in a population of number density N has encounter rate Γ=πR2N⟨vrel​⟩. A Poisson process gives merger probability 1−e−ΓT, approximated by ΓT only for rare encounters. Counts of distinct pairs across the whole population additionally require a factor of one-half.

Words: 101 Articles: 1
Galaxy merger OurBigBook.com
Tidal capture converts sufficient relative orbital energy into internal tidal heating to leave two initially unbound galaxies on a bound orbit. For identical spherical galaxies of mass mg​, a distant rapid flyby of impact parameter p and relative speed v gives the approximate capture condition pv<[(32/3)G2mg2​⟨r2⟩]1/4. This requires the impulse approximation and weak gravitational focusing; it is not a general criterion for subsequent coalescence.

Tidal capture of galaxies OurBigBook.com
Two equal galaxies each receive the tidal impulse heating of a spherical galaxy, while their relative orbital energy at infinity is mg​v2/4. Transfer of more internal energy than that orbital energy gives pv<[32G2mg2​⟨r2⟩/3]1/4. Slow encounters require adiabatic shielding of tidal encounters, so the impulsive inequality does not apply there.

Galaxy merger OurBigBook.com
A dry galaxy merger joins galaxies with little cold gas, so dissipation and merger-triggered star formation are weak. Conservation of energy followed by re-virialization can make repeated dry minor mergers increase a galaxy's radius faster than its mass.

Dry galaxy merger OurBigBook.com
In a dry galaxy merger, zero orbital energy at infinite separation and retention of all mass and energy give EF​=EI​+EA​. If the progenitors and remnant satisfy the virial theorem, their gravitational radii obey RF​/RI​=(1+η)2/(1+ϵη), where η=MA​/MI​ and ϵ=⟨vA2​⟩/⟨vI2​⟩. The latter average is weighted by satellite mass. Nonzero orbital energy, escaping stars, or dissipative losses change the energy accounting.

Minor galaxy merger OurBigBook.com
For repeated minor galaxy mergers with negligible internal satellite binding energy and zero orbital energy at infinity, parabolic dry-merger energy accounting leaves total energy nearly constant. A surface-density limit is not a universal ceiling on total star formation rate: the star-forming area matters. Radiation-supported starburst disk calculations give characteristic optically thick infrared fluxes near 1013L⊙​kpc−2.

Words: 126 Articles: 1

Take an initially isolated virialized self-gravitating stellar population with kinetic energy T=∣W∣/2 and Newtonian gravitational potential energy W<0. Instantaneous spatially uniform removal of mass, without kicks to surviving material, leaves fraction f with T′=fT and W′=f2W. Hence E′=∣W∣f(1/2−f): the homologous whole-system energy is negative only for f>1/2. Positive whole-system energy does not forbid a bound core after selective escape, and slow mass loss follows the adiabatic mass-loss expansion law instead.

An alpha element is an element such as oxygen, neon or magnesium associated with nucleosynthesis involving helium nuclei and massive-star burning. Words: 63
Alpha element OurBigBook.com
Massive stars produce prompt enrichment through core-collapse supernovae, whereas a Type Ia supernova follows binary stellar evolution and contributes substantial iron after a distribution of delays. A stellar population formed rapidly before much delayed enrichment can have a larger alpha-element to iron ratio than a stellar population formed over a prolonged interval. Relative abundance also depends on the initial mass function, stellar yields, and gas exchange; this is a chemical clock with model assumptions.
